status: Under investigation. Labelled suspected exposure with investigation ongoing, reflecting SBI's own statement that the count is preliminary and that authenticity and extent remain to be established.
quantitative_claims: 3,897 SBI customer records containing PII identified, per the exchange filing [S116] | Approximately 375,000 records available on the dark web, within which the 3,897 were identified [S116] | Alert received 16 October 2026 from the Bank's Threat Intelligence Service Provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In [S116] | An independent CERT-In-empanelled cybersecurity agency was engaged to assess the compromise [S116] | Bank operations continued to operate normally without disruptions [S116] | Data fields: mobile number, date of birth, name, gender, email, residential address, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, loan/lead metadata [S051]
remaining_unknowns: Whether the data is authentic. | The source of the exposure - whether SBI, a vendor, or an aggregation of other breaches. | The full extent of exposure. | What the remaining approximately 371,000 records in the dataset relate to.
disputed_claims: Headlines stating that SBI was hacked overstate the evidence. What is established is that records attributed to SBI customers appeared in a dark-web dataset; the source is undetermined and SBI has not confirmed a breach of its own systems. | The 375,000-record dataset total has in places been reported as the SBI exposure. SBI identified 3,897 records as its own.
lessons: Dark-web monitoring regularly finds data attributed to an organisation before any internal breach is identified; the attribution itself requires verification. | A bank being alerted by its own threat-intelligence provider, a national CERT and a defence agency simultaneously shows coordinated monitoring working as intended. | Disclosing a preliminary count while stating that authenticity is unverified is responsible practice, and should be reported with the same caveats the bank applied.

title: Bullhorn takes its staffing platform offline to contain a cyberattack
orgs: Bullhorn; more than 10,000 customer organisations
evidence_label_meaning: Confirmed by affected organisation or authority
root_cause: Not disclosed.
impact: System-wide outage across Bullhorn's core products affecting a customer base of more than 10,000 organisations, with consequent disruption to recruitment and payroll-adjacent operations. Data exfiltration undetermined.
attribution: Unattributed.
attribution_confidence: No actor named; CrowdStrike engaged for investigation.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported.
status: Containment by platform shutdown; recovery ongoing with no published restoration timeline at the time of the latest reviewed source. Exfiltration undetermined.
quantitative_claims: More than 10,000 global customers affected by the outage [S048] | Services offline: ATS/CRM, Automation, Back Office, Talent Platform [S048] | Exfiltration status: not yet determined [S048]
remaining_unknowns: Entry point and root cause. | Whether customer data was exfiltrated. | Restoration timeline. | Whether the password resets indicate credential compromise or were purely precautionary.
disputed_claims: The outage was Bullhorn's containment decision. Describing the platform as 'taken down by hackers' misstates a precautionary shutdown as attacker-caused destruction.
lessons: Taking a platform fully offline is a severe but sometimes correct containment choice; customers need pre-agreed expectations and data-export routes for that scenario. | Password resets for non-SSO users indicate where identity consolidation would have reduced response cost - SSO users were not reset. | Recruitment platforms hold candidate identity documents and employment records, so an undetermined exfiltration status carries substantial latent privacy risk. | Separating a security incident from subsequent routine maintenance in public communications prevents a false causal narrative forming.

title: PHP2Shell: two critical unauthenticated RCE vulnerabilities in PHP trigger a global emergency patching event
orgs: The PHP Group; operators of PHP-based web infrastructure worldwide
evidence_label_meaning: Vulnerability emergency without established victim compromise
first_disclosure_date: 2026-10-20 (advance notice and research disclosure); 2026-10-21 14:00 UTC (coordinated disclosure and patches)
chronology_basis: Occurrence: earliest observed exploitation attempts, 17 October 2026
root_cause: Improper handling of fatal errors, particularly out-of-memory conditions, leaving corrupted or stale internal engine state that later request processing trusts. The flaws are at engine level and independent of application code.
impact: Potential unauthenticated remote code execution and worker-memory disclosure across a very large share of the web. Realised impact in the period covered is dominated not by confirmed compromises but by defensive disruption: large-scale emergency patching and precautionary service shutdowns (see OCT26-020). No confirmed victim compromise attributable to PHP2Shell was established in the sources read.
attribution: Multiple distinct actors. AWS assessed multiple actors from varying payloads and choices of anonymisation infrastructure, with attempts originating from commercial anonymisation networks. No actor is named.
attribution_confidence: AWS expressed moderate confidence, and acknowledged uncertainty about how threat actors obtained exploit information before disclosure.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement is established in the discovery or exploitation of these vulnerabilities in the primary sources read. Some secondary commentary has linked PHP2Shell's discovery to AI-assisted research; that claim is not substantiated by the PHP Group, Wiz, AWS or CISA material reviewed, and is recorded as unresolved in the corrections section rather than asserted here.
status: Patched upstream on 21 October 2026. Exploitation attempts broad and ongoing. AWS stated it is unclear whether any observed attempt would have succeeded against real-world systems, and found no confirmed successful compromises. watchTowr reported observing in-the-wild exploitation while noting that an attack needs specific knowledge of the target server and specific conditions, and that public exploits do not work against a default PHP installation. A further PHP advisory on 23 October covered CVE-2026-115560, an unrelated session upload-progress issue arising only under unusual configuration.
quantitative_claims: 2 CVEs: CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619; CVSS v4.0 9.2 [S024][S025] | Affected: every PHP release in the last decade, back to PHP 5.4 [S025] | Patched releases, 21 October 2026: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35, plus 8.6.0 RC4 [S024] | Embargo lift: 21 October 2026, 14:00 UTC [S024][S026] | Pre-disclosure exploitation attempts observed by Amazon MadPot: 17 October 2026, four days before disclosure [S026] | Earliest public proof-of-concept: about 02:00 UTC on 21 October, roughly 12 hours before embargo lift [S026] | Demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against current WordPress, Drupal and Joomla images (research) [S025] | CISA position on 21 October: had not observed exploitation [S027] | Confirmed successful real-world compromises: none established in sources read
remaining_unknowns: How attackers obtained exploit information four days before coordinated disclosure. | Whether any real-world system was successfully compromised via PHP2Shell. | The true volume of exploitation attempts. The Guardian reported millions of attempts, but that source was not retrievable by this tooling and the figure is therefore not relied on here. | How many internet-facing PHP installations remain unpatched.
disputed_claims: Exploitation attempts have been widely reported as successful compromises. AWS explicitly declined to say the attempts would have succeeded, and CISA stated on 21 October that it had not observed exploitation. | Claims that PHP2Shell was found using OpenAI technology circulated in October coverage. No primary source read for this report substantiates that, and it is listed as an unresolved question. | A vulnerable product's installation count is not a victim count. PHP's ubiquity bounds potential exposure, not realised harm.
lessons: Pre-disclosure exploitation four days before embargo lift means coordinated disclosure windows are themselves a risk period; detection should not wait for the advisory. | Engine-level flaws bypass application hardening entirely - WAF rules and application controls offered limited protection where execution precedes application code. | Worker-memory disclosure means that patching alone is insufficient where exposure is suspected: credentials resident in worker memory should be rotated. | End-of-life PHP versions received no fix. PHP 8.1 and earlier required taking systems offline, which is a lifecycle-management failure surfacing as an incident. | A 9.2-rated flaw that is hard to exploit in default configurations still produces enormous defensive cost. Severity drives response effort regardless of realised exploitation.

title: eMudhra / emSign certificate authority: weak keys let anyone recover private keys; browsers block eight intermediates
orgs: eMudhra (emSign CA); Mozilla; Google; Apple; Go project and Linux distributions
evidence_label_meaning: Confirmed by affected organisation or authority
chronology_basis: October disclosure and vendor action; underlying key generation April 2025
root_cause: A key-generation error produced a second set of cryptographically weak P-384 keys with values below 256. Because their labels resembled those of the correctly generated keys, the weak keys were mistakenly selected for certificate signing.
impact: Latent capability for any party to forge publicly trusted certificates for arbitrary websites, enabling impersonation and interception. eMudhra reports no evidence that the affected intermediates were used to issue end-user certificates, and states most were never used in production. No confirmed misuse or interception attack has been reported.
attribution: No adversary. This is an operational and cryptographic failure by the certificate authority.
attribution_confidence: Root cause acknowledged by eMudhra itself.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement.
status: Mitigated by browser and library vendors between 17 and 22 October 2026. eMudhra reported no evidence of end-user certificate issuance from the affected intermediates. Reporting indicates eMudhra exited the SSL/TLS business. CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0050, retrieved on 24 October 2026, records that only one of the eight affected intermediates had been deployed in production, that they were revoked on 18 October 2026, that eMudhra's domestic Indian DSC and eSign infrastructure was unaffected through architectural isolation, and that Google's removal of emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store was expected to reach devices on 27 October 2026 [S037].
quantitative_claims: 8 intermediate certificates affected [S038] | Private key values smaller than 256, recoverable by testing 256 candidates [S038] | Keys generated April 2025; mitigations completed 22 October 2026 - about 18 months of exposure [S038] | Chrome blocked 6 compromised intermediates on 17 October 2026 [S038] | Demonstration private key value published by a researcher: 4 [S038] | Related software tracking identifier: CVE-2026-111943 (Go 1.27.3, 1.26.10) [S038] | Confirmed mis-issued end-user certificates: none reported [S038]
remaining_unknowns: Whether any certificate was ever forged using them. | How the label-similarity selection error passed the CA's key-ceremony and audit controls. | Whether anyone other than the reporting researcher recovered the keys during the eighteen-month window. CERT-In records that no TLS certificates chaining to the six affected TLS intermediates appear in Certificate Transparency logs, which is strong negative evidence but not proof of non-use [S037].
disputed_claims: Some coverage described this as a CA breach or hack. There is no adversary: it is a key-generation and key-selection failure, which the CA has acknowledged. | That the keys were recoverable is confirmed; that they were abused is not evidenced.
lessons: Key-generation output must be validated against expected entropy and magnitude before a key is ever eligible for signing - a value below 256 in a P-384 slot should be impossible to use. | Naming and labelling conventions are a security control in a key-management system; similar labels for weak and strong keys invited exactly this substitution. | The web PKI's recovery path worked quickly once the issue was public: browser blocks landed within days across three vendors. | An eighteen-month undetected exposure in a trust anchor argues for continuous external scanning of issued-certificate key quality, not only point-in-time audits.

title: OpenCode Console breach exposes stored external AI-provider API keys
orgs: OpenCode; OpenCode Console users with external providers linked (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google)
itype: Credential exposure; abuse of stolen API keys for model distillation
evidence_label_meaning: Credibly reported, not independently confirmed
chronology_basis: Occurrence: earliest exposure date given by the project
root_cause: Not disclosed. The maintainer's statement describes the outcome - exposure of stored external-provider API keys - without identifying the intrusion vector into OpenCode's own systems.
impact: Exposure of external-provider API keys for 1.4 percent of OpenCode Console users who had linked providers, with consequent unauthorised consumption billed to those users. Reported individual charges run from several hundred to about 1,700 US dollars. No verified aggregate loss, and no statement that all refunds have been completed.
attribution: Unattributed. No actor named.
attribution_confidence: No attribution offered by OpenCode or by the reporting.
ai_evidence: AI use is substantiated on the attacker's side and is the point of the attack: the stolen keys were used to drive model distillation at scale. The affected asset is also AI infrastructure. This is one of the few incidents in the register where AI is simultaneously the target, the tool and the motive.
status: Disclosed 19 October 2026; impacted users notified by email. Labelled credibly reported rather than confirmed because the maintainer's statement is relayed through secondary reporting and the original social post was not retrieved directly.
quantitative_claims: 1.4% of OpenCode Console users impacted - specifically those with external providers linked [S113] | Providers involved: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google [S113] | Earliest exposure: 17 October 2026 [S113] | Attackers targeted the systems for at least 48 hours [S113] | User-reported unauthorised charges: several hundred to approximately 1,700 USD overnight; individual reports, not audited [S113] | Aggregate loss figure published by OpenCode: none [S113]
remaining_unknowns: The intrusion vector into OpenCode's systems. | The absolute number of affected users, since only a percentage was published. | The total unauthorised spend across all victims. | Whether affected users were reimbursed by the providers. | Why external-provider API keys were retrievable in a usable form rather than held so the service could use them without reading them back.
disputed_claims: The 1.4% figure applies to OpenCode Console users with external providers linked. It is not 1.4% of all OpenCode installations, nor of all developers, and should not be restated as either. | The charge figures are individual user reports on social media. No audited total exists, and no source establishes that all refunds were completed.
lessons: A service that stores third-party API keys is a credential aggregator, and its compromise bills the victim directly, because provider keys are spending authority as much as access. | Distillation gives stolen model credentials a monetisation path that needs no buyer, only throughput, which changes the economics of this kind of theft. | Provider-side anomaly detection caught the abuse in some accounts before the victims did, which argues for per-key spend limits and alerting held at the provider account rather than at the storing service. | Keys held for convenience should be stored so the service can use them without being able to return them in plaintext.

title: United States education sector: ransomware and network incidents disrupt several school districts and a medical school
orgs: Jerome School District (Idaho); Oneonta City School District (New York); Llano Independent School District (Texas); Richmond Public Schools (Virginia); Easthampton Public Schools (Massachusetts); University of Illinois Chicago College of Medicine
itype: Ransomware; network intrusion; OT/building systems impact
evidence_label_meaning: Credibly reported, not independently confirmed
chronology_basis: Occurrence date of the earliest dated incident in the group
root_cause: Various and largely undisclosed.
impact: School closures and lost instructional days; loss of physical access control and climate control at Jerome; data theft at UIC College of Medicine. No verified record counts.
attribution: Qilin (Llano ISD claim); Booba Project (UIC claim). Others unattributed.
attribution_confidence: Both named attributions are attacker self-claims on leak sites.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported.
status: Variously under investigation and recovering. Labelled credibly reported; the volume claims are attacker claims. No institutional notice was retrieved for any of these within the research window.
quantitative_claims: Jerome School District: classes cancelled 19 and 20 October 2026; cameras, door locks and climate controls affected [S100] | Oneonta City School District: ransomware discovered 22 October; closures 23 and 26 October 2026 [S094 discovery] | Llano ISD: Qilin claim posted 18 October 2026 [S109] | UIC College of Medicine: 344 GB claimed stolen by Booba Project (attacker claim) [S101]
remaining_unknowns: Entry points and root causes. | Whether student or patient data was exfiltrated and in what volume. | Recovery timelines. | Whether the attacker volume claims are accurate.
disputed_claims: The 344 GB figure for UIC is an attacker claim. | The Llano ISD entry rests on a Qilin leak-site posting, not on a district disclosure.
lessons: An IT network intrusion that reaches door locks and climate control becomes a child-safety matter, which is why Jerome closed rather than merely degraded service. | School districts lose instructional days as their primary impact metric, which conventional breach reporting does not capture. | Teaching hospitals and medical schools hold research and patient-adjacent data under university-grade rather than hospital-grade controls.

title: ARTEX traces found on attack infrastructure targeting about 20 Japanese companies
orgs: GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae (investigator); about 20 Japanese companies, 8 of which disclosed breaches
evidence_label_meaning: Researcher-observed / researcher-assessed
chronology_basis: October research disclosure linking earlier breaches to shared AI tooling
root_cause: Exploitation of known vulnerabilities and exposed or under-protected APIs, discovered at scale with AI assistance. Mobile application packages were mined to find the APIs worth attacking.
impact: Eight of approximately 20 targeted Japanese companies disclosed breaches. The investigators' contribution is the linkage of these otherwise separate disclosures to shared AI-enabled attack infrastructure, not a new victim count.
attribution: Unattributed to a named actor. The tool, ARTEX, is Chinese-developed and openly available; the investigators identify tooling, not an operator.
attribution_confidence: Researcher assessment by GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae, based on infrastructure analysis. Tool provenance is not actor attribution, and no state linkage is claimed for the Japanese campaign.
ai_evidence: ARTEX traces were found directly on the attack infrastructure, and the described techniques - automated vulnerability scanning and API attack at scale - are consistent with agentic tooling. The AI use is attributed to the attacker.
status: Published finding. Individual victim organisations are at varying stages of their own response (see the Japan cluster incidents in this register).
quantitative_claims: About 20 Japanese companies targeted by the identified infrastructure [S074][S075] | 8 of those approximately 20 had publicly disclosed breaches [S074][S075] | Multiple attack servers identified carrying mobile-app and web-application offensive tooling [S074]
remaining_unknowns: Which eight disclosed breaches correspond to the roughly 20 targeted companies. The mapping is not public, so no incident in this register is attributed to this campaign individually. | Whether one operator or several used the infrastructure. | Whether there is any relationship to Storm-0940 (OCT26-001) beyond shared use of an openly available framework. | How much of Japan's wider October disclosure surge this campaign accounts for.
disputed_claims: This finding has been reported as explaining Japan's entire October breach wave. It covers about 20 targeted companies and eight disclosed breaches - a subset. At least 36 Japanese organisations issued first breach notices between 25 September and 8 October alone [S075]. | Shared use of an open-source framework does not make separate intrusions one campaign, and does not establish a common operator with Storm-0940.
lessons: Mobile application packages are a map of an organisation's API attack surface, and are trivially obtainable; APIs reachable only via an app still need to be defended as internet-facing. | Tool-based clustering is genuinely useful for linking apparently unrelated breaches, but it establishes shared tooling rather than shared authorship. | An openly available offensive framework appearing in China-state-aligned activity, independent criminal activity in Japan, and suspected activity in South Korea illustrates how quickly capability diffuses once published.

title: CISA, FBI and international partners issue a joint advisory on SafePay ransomware affecting at least 600 organisations
orgs: CISA; FBI; US Secret Service; Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz (Germany); UK National Crime Agency and North West Regional Organised Crime Unit; SafePay ransomware group
itype: Law enforcement / government advisory on an active ransomware campaign
evidence_label_meaning: Confirmed by affected organisation or authority
chronology_basis: October advisory publication date; underlying campaign ongoing since August 2024
root_cause: Initial access via credential exposure, brute-force password attacks and VPN access exploitation. These are credential and remote-access weaknesses rather than software vulnerabilities.
impact: At least 600 organisations affected cumulatively since August 2024 across four continents and multiple critical infrastructure sectors. The advisory's purpose is defensive guidance, not the disclosure of a new incident.
attribution: SafePay ransomware group, named by the issuing agencies.
attribution_confidence: Multi-agency law enforcement attribution of a criminal group. No state sponsorship is alleged.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported in the advisory as summarised.
status: Advisory published with mitigation guidance. The campaign is ongoing. No arrests or disruption action is reported in the sources reviewed.
quantitative_claims: Advisory identifier: AA26-293A, published 20 October 2026 [S086] | At least 600 organisations affected since August 2024 (cumulative, not October) [S086][S087] | Regions: North America, South America, Europe, Australia [S086] | Partners: CISA, FBI, US Secret Service, Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, UK NCA and North West ROCU [S086]
remaining_unknowns: The composition of the 600 victims by sector and country. | Total ransom payments. | Whether any disruption operation is under way. | How the group's use of Mullvad VPN infrastructure is being addressed.
disputed_claims: The 600-organisation figure is cumulative since August 2024. Reporting it as an October figure would be wrong, and it is excluded from this report's October incident counts.
lessons: Credential exposure and brute-forceable remote access still underpin high-volume ransomware operations; no novel technique is required at 600 victims. | Commercial VPN infrastructure used as attacker egress complicates IP-based blocking, since the same addresses carry legitimate privacy traffic. | Direct telephone contact with victims is an escalation in extortion pressure that organisations should prepare staff for. | Cumulative advisory totals must be kept out of period-specific incident counts.

title: LiteLLM release pipeline compromised; malicious v1.107.0 published to PyPI, Docker Hub and GHCR
orgs: LiteLLM (BerriAI); downstream users of litellm 1.107.0
sector: AI developer tooling; software supply chain
evidence_label_meaning: Confirmed by affected organisation or authority
ai_role_meaning: AI system affected, but AI use by attacker unproven
root_cause: An Agent Platform master key committed publicly to the LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository on 27 May 2026 and never revoked. Reuse of that key on 10 October yielded a GitHub organisation owner's OAuth token, which was escalated to further maintainer tokens and ultimately to control of the release workflow.
impact: Any environment that installed or ran litellm 1.107.0 with internet access must be treated as having had its credentials exposed. LiteLLM's guidance is unambiguous: rotate everything, including IAM roles, API keys and database credentials. Because LiteLLM sits in front of model providers, the credentials most at risk are precisely the high-value model and cloud keys it brokers. No downstream victim count has been published.
attribution: Unattributed. No actor named.
attribution_confidence: No attribution offered by LiteLLM or by the independent analysts.
ai_evidence: LiteLLM is AI infrastructure and the credentials at risk are largely model-provider keys, so an AI system was the affected asset. There is no evidence that the attacker used AI to conduct the intrusion. Classified as AI system affected, AI use by attacker unproven.
status: Contained the same day. Malicious artefacts removed from all three registries within about four and a half hours of the first upload. Users must manually delete the dropped files, kill the Python daemon, reinstall pinned to v1.106.2, and rotate all credentials if 1.107.0 ever ran with internet access.
quantitative_claims: PyPI: litellm==1.107.0, all seven wheels, live 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC (about 1h43m) [S034] | Docker Hub: tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable compromised 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC (about 2h33m) [S034] | GHCR: same tags pointing to three compromised image indexes, 11:46:56 to 13:51 UTC (about 2h04m) [S034] | Master key committed publicly 27 May 2026; never revoked [S034B] | Key reused 10 October 2026, 21:13-21:28 UTC, from IP 69.48.229.143 [S034B] | Malicious release published 21 October at 11:11:18 UTC after production-gate approval [S034B] | Malicious artefacts dropped: cook.pth, cook.py, sitecustomize.py [S034] | No download or victim count published [S034]
remaining_unknowns: How many environments installed or ran the malicious version. | What credentials were actually exfiltrated, and whether any have been used. | Why the master key was never revoked in the nearly five months it sat in a public repository. | Whether any party other than this attacker found and used the exposed key during that window. | What was done with the secrets exfiltrated from private repositories on 12 October.
disputed_claims: LiteLLM's initial incident page suspected the attacker took GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from the logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment. The canonical 23 October attack-chain report states this was inaccurate: the first token came from the Agent Platform API, reached with a master key exposed publicly on 27 May 2026. The vendor's own wording is that 'some assumptions and beliefs in those updates were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete'. This record follows the canonical report; earlier reporting repeating the log theory is superseded [S034B].
lessons: A secret committed to a public repository is compromised from that moment. The gap here was not detection of the commit but the absence of revocation across the following five months. | Credential inventory has to include keys that grant access to internal agent platforms, which are often newer than the secret-scanning rules pointed at them. | One master key yielded an organisation owner's token, which yielded two more maintainer tokens, which yielded the release pipeline. Blast radius follows the first key, not the last. | An exposure window of under two hours is still a full compromise for anyone who pulled during it; 'latest' and 'main-stable' tags propagate immediately into CI. | A gateway that brokers credentials concentrates them. Compromise of AI middleware yields the keys to every model and cloud account behind it.

title: Railway detects unauthorised access to customer environment variables; some decrypted
orgs: Railway (developer cloud platform); a subset of Railway customers
evidence_label_meaning: Suspected exposure; investigation ongoing
root_cause: Not disclosed.
impact: Potential exposure of secrets for a subset of Railway customers, with downstream risk to every third-party service whose credentials were stored on the platform. Deployments were paused, which is a direct operational impact on customers. No confirmed count of affected customers or of exfiltrated secrets has been published.
attribution: Unattributed.
attribution_confidence: No actor named by Railway.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported on either side of this incident.
status: Investigation ongoing as of the latest reviewed disclosure. Deployments were paused on 21 October; the status page was still being updated at the research cutoff. Affected accounts to be contacted individually. Because the company's own language is 'may have accessed', this is recorded as suspected exposure with investigation ongoing.
quantitative_claims: Affected population described only as 'a subset of users' [S031] | No count of exposed or decrypted variables published [S031] | All deployments paused during investigation [S031]
remaining_unknowns: The entry point and root cause - not disclosed. | How many customers and how many variables were affected. | How decryption was achieved for 'some' variables, which implies key access rather than ciphertext theft alone. | Whether any exposed credential has been used against a downstream service. | Whether the 22 October AWS and GCP anomalies are consequences of this incident or separate findings.
disputed_claims: Some coverage characterised this as a confirmed breach of all Railway secrets. Railway's own wording is narrower: potential access to encrypted variables, with decrypted contents obtained for some.
lessons: A platform that stores and decrypts customer secrets is a credential aggregator; its compromise is a supply-chain event for every downstream service. | Rotate-everything guidance is only actionable if customers already know what secrets they hold and where those secrets are used. Secret inventory is the prerequisite. | That ciphertext was decrypted for some variables implies the encryption keys were reachable from the compromised path - envelope encryption only helps if the key custodian is separately protected. | Pausing deployments is a legitimate containment trade-off, and should be recognised as a precautionary action by the provider rather than attacker-caused destruction.

title: GitLab patches CVE-2026-110264, a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated RCE affecting twelve years of releases
orgs: GitLab; operators of self-managed GitLab Community and Enterprise Edition
evidence_label_meaning: Vulnerability emergency without established victim compromise
root_cause: An integer overflow in the regular expression compiler, allowing an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. The affected code path has been present since GitLab 7.0 (2014) [S115].
impact: Potential unauthenticated remote code execution on self-managed GitLab servers. No exploitation or victim compromise reported. GitLab.com SaaS was not identified as affected in the reviewed reporting.
attribution: Not applicable - no exploitation reported.
attribution_confidence: Not applicable.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported.
status: Patched 21 October 2026. No observed exploitation as of the cutoff.
quantitative_claims: CVE-2026-110264; CVSS 10.0; integer overflow in the regular expression compiler [S115] | Affected: GitLab CE/EE 7.0 through 19.4.2, plus 19.5.0 [S115] | Fixed in 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13 [S115] | GitLab.com was already running the patched version [S115] | GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0 / 19.4.2-internal0 or later needed no action [S115] | Affected code present since GitLab 7.0 (2014) - about 12 years of releases [S081] | Patched 21 October 2026 [S081] | Not in the CISA KEV catalog as of 22 October 2026 [S081] | Evidence of exploitation: none [S081]
remaining_unknowns: Technical specifics of the vulnerable code path. | How many self-managed instances remain unpatched. | Whether the flaw was ever exploited during the twelve years it was present.
disputed_claims: A twelve-year vulnerable window is not twelve years of exploitation. No evidence of historical exploitation exists, and the sources say so explicitly.
lessons: Self-managed developer platforms are supply-chain infrastructure; unauthenticated RCE there is equivalent to compromising everything they build and deploy. | Patch prioritisation driven by news volume rather than severity would have deferred a CVSS 10.0 flaw in favour of a 9.2 one, purely because the latter dominated coverage. | Absence from the KEV catalog means no observed exploitation, not low risk.

title: Governments and institutions worldwide take websites offline as a precaution against PHP2Shell
orgs: Government bodies in Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Finland and Czechia; schools, hospitals and other organisations; CERT-EU; Japanese government
itype: Precautionary service withdrawal in response to a vulnerability emergency
evidence_label_meaning: Vulnerability emergency without established victim compromise
root_cause: Precautionary response to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (OCT26-017).
impact: Widespread loss of availability of public-facing government and institutional services across multiple countries. The impact is real but self-inflicted and protective. No compromise of the affected bodies is reported as the cause of any shutdown.
attribution: Not applicable - no attacker involvement in these outages.
attribution_confidence: Not applicable.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement.
status: Services progressively restored as patching completed. Japan was reported on 23 October to be planning cyberattack simulation exercises in the wake of the PHP flaws.
quantitative_claims: At least 6 countries took government websites offline: Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Finland, Czechia [S082] | Additional affected categories: schools, hospitals and other organisations across Europe [S082] | CERT-EU urgent alert issued 21 October 2026 [S083] | Japan: Prime Ministerial request posted 21:55 JST, 21 October 2026, ahead of the 23:00 JST patch release [S090] | Confirmed exploitation as a cause of any shutdown: none reported [S082]
remaining_unknowns: The total number of websites withdrawn worldwide. | How long individual services remained offline. | Whether any organisation that withdrew a service later found evidence of prior compromise.
disputed_claims: This event has been widely rendered as governments being knocked offline by a cyberattack. Every reported shutdown was precautionary, and officials said there were no indications of active exploitation at the time. | The 'Black October' framing draws heavily on these outages. They are evidence of a severe vulnerability and of decisive defensive action - not of mass successful intrusion.
lessons: Taking a service offline is a legitimate, sometimes optimal control when a patch cannot be applied fast enough. It should be planned for, not improvised. | A head of government issuing direct patching instructions is a notable escalation in how states communicate cyber risk to the public. | Organisations that could not rapidly inventory their PHP estate were forced into blanket shutdowns; asset inventory determined whether the response was surgical or total. | Analysts must keep precautionary withdrawal distinct from attacker-caused outage, or incident statistics become meaningless.

title: Quest Diagnostics discloses unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform
orgs: Quest Diagnostics
evidence_label_meaning: Suspected exposure; investigation ongoing
root_cause: Not disclosed. Quest stated the incident is unrelated to the PHP vulnerabilities.
impact: Believed access to certain patient records, including patient health information and patient-identifiable information. Platform access suspended, disrupting test ordering and results retrieval for client providers. Scope and affected-individual count undetermined.
attribution: Unattributed.
attribution_confidence: No actor named; federal law enforcement notified.
ai_evidence: No AI involvement reported.
status: Under active investigation as of the cutoff, two days after discovery. Platform access suspended. Scope being determined; HIPAA notification obligations would follow once scope is established.
quantitative_claims: Discovery date: 21 October 2026 [S084][S085] | Affected-individual count: not determined at disclosure [S084][S085] | Data categories: patient health information and patient-identifiable information [S085] | Platform access suspended [S085] | Relationship to the PHP vulnerabilities: none, per Quest [S085]
remaining_unknowns: Entry point and root cause. | How many patients are affected. | How long the unauthorised access persisted before discovery. | Whether data was exfiltrated as opposed to accessed.
disputed_claims: Some coverage attached specific large patient figures to this incident. Quest published no affected-individual count, and this report does not supply one. | Because it surfaced on 21-22 October, this incident was linked by some commentary to PHP2Shell. Quest expressly denied that connection.
lessons: Clinical ordering and results platforms sit between provider and patient; suspending one has immediate care-delivery consequences, making containment decisions clinically significant. | Securities disclosure obligations now drive rapid public reporting of cyber incidents, often before scope is known - readers should expect initial figures to be absent rather than reassuring. | Explicitly ruling out a high-profile concurrent vulnerability, as Quest did, is useful and prevents a false causal narrative.

title: Major U.S. banks detect unauthorised third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts
orgs: Morgan Stanley; JPMorgan Chase; Bank of America; Citi; Wells Fargo; Charles Schwab; PNC; U.S. Bancorp
itype: Unauthorised automated access; policy violation; agentic-AI access control
evidence_label_meaning: Credibly reported, not independently confirmed
detection_date: Unknown; banks describe ongoing detection and blocking
chronology_basis: October disclosure date; underlying activity period not established
root_cause: Customers supplying their own banking credentials to third-party AI agents, combined with the banks' inability to distinguish agent sessions from human customer sessions. No software vulnerability is reported.
impact: Operational and governance impact: institutions are blocking agent sessions and restricting access. No confirmed financial loss, completed unauthorised transaction, or compromise of bank systems is reported in any source reviewed. Charles Schwab's chief executive described blocking unauthorised AI agents a double-digit number of times every week, which indicates volume of blocked attempts, not successful intrusions.
attribution: No threat actor. The agents are commercial or personal AI assistants acting on customer-supplied credentials; this is not characterised as criminal activity by any source reviewed.
attribution_confidence: Not applicable - no adversary attribution is claimed by any party.
ai_evidence: AI agents are the subject of the incident and their involvement is directly reported by the banks themselves. However, the AI systems here are acting on legitimately supplied credentials, not attacking the banks.
status: Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting agent access. Citi does not permit third-party agents to log in or transact. Industry position as reported is that human-in-the-loop approval and regulatory change are prerequisites for sanctioned agent transactions.
quantitative_claims: Charles Schwab: blocking unauthorised AI agents 'a double-digit number of times every week' - CEO Rick Wurster [S006] | No incident count, affected-account count, or loss figure was published by any bank [S005][S006]
remaining_unknowns: When this activity began and over what period it has been occurring. | How many accounts or customers are involved. | Which specific agent products or vendors are responsible. | What the agents actually did when they 'acted independently of user instructions', in concrete terms. | Whether any transaction was ever completed without customer authorisation.
disputed_claims: A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the bank had not observed instances of 'rogue AI agents accessing our platforms', which sits in tension with the framing that Morgan Stanley is blocking such agents [S005]. Both statements are reported from the same source and are presented here together rather than reconciled. | The 23 October Axios follow-up indicates that banks' investment in prevention is driven by concerns about frontier AI systems rather than by these agent incidents, and distinguishes this activity from the July 2026 Hugging Face agent-swarm episode (see HIST-02). That clarification materially narrows the 22 October story. It is recorded here with the caveat that [S007] returned HTTP 403 and was not read in full. | Secondary and social coverage repeatedly escalated this into 'banks hacked by AI'. No reviewed source supports that.
lessons: Credential sharing with an agent transfers the full authority of the accountholder, with no scoping and no revocation path short of a password change. | Terms-of-service prohibitions are not an access control; if agent access is undesirable it has to be detected and blocked technically. | The sector needs scoped, revocable, auditable delegation - a recognised agent identity with explicit permissions - rather than a binary human-or-blocked model. | Distinguish carefully between an agent exceeding its instructions and an adversary attacking a bank; the defensive response differs entirely.
